title: Functional diversity and ecological consequences of endophytic  Bacillus –plant interactions
abstract: Abstract The genus  Bacillus , particularly endophytic species, has been widely studied as a source of plant growth-promoting bacteria in agricultural systems. These microorganisms contribute to plant performance through nutrient acquisition, phytohormone production, pathogen suppression, microbiome modulation, and enhanced tolerance to biotic and abiotic stresses. However, their ecological roles, functional plasticity, and genomic diversity remain poorly integrated into conceptual frameworks that extend beyond crop-based applications. Functional plasticity is reflected in their ability to colonize diverse plant hosts and tissues and to promote similar plant responses through distinct molecular mechanisms. Likewise, genomic diversity is evidenced by variation in accessory genomes, biosynthetic gene clusters, and regulatory networks that shape ecological functions and metabolite production. This review examines endophytic  Bacillus  as a model for understanding how metabolically versatile and genomically plastic bacteria establish functional, but context-dependent, associations with plants. Drawing on evidence from functional genomics, pangenomics, metabolomics, and microbial ecology, we discuss mechanisms associated with plant growth promotion and emphasize their dependence on host identity, environmental conditions, and microbial interactions. We address functional convergence arising from distinct genetic and metabolic routes, the contribution of accessory genomes and regulatory variation, and the ecological consequences of microbial inoculation in resident plant-associated microbiomes. We also highlight the limitations of in vitro screening approaches and the need for experimental validation across multiple biological scales to establish robust genotype–phenotype relationships. Finally, we extend the discussion beyond agricultural systems to consider the use of endophytic  Bacillus  in wild plant systems and ecological restoration, emphasizing the importance of evaluating both functional outcomes and ecological impacts.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The genus  Bacillus  comprises Gram-positive bacteria of the phylum Bacillota (Firmicutes), characterized by their ability to form endospores and their wide distribution across diverse natural environments (Patel and Gupta,  173 ; Harirchi et al.  87 ). These bacteria can be found in soil (Aslim et al.  17 ), water (Yoon et al.  252 ), and extreme environments such as alkaline lakes (Guadie et al.  82 ), hypersaline lakes (Amoozegar et al.  9 ), and hot springs (Panda et al.  170 ). In general,  Bacillus  spp. are metabolically versatile, capable of growing on a broad range of substrates and under varied temperature conditions, from approximately 10 °C to over 50 °C (Mendo et al.  148 ,  149 ; Guérin et al.  83 ; Harirchi et al.  87 ). Additionally, different species within the genus can establish diverse ecological interactions with other organisms, ranging from antagonistic relationships to mutualistic associations. Species belonging to the  Bacillus cereus  sensu lato group, for instance, can be pathogenic to humans, causing illnesses that range from food poisoning (Jovanovic et al.  102 ; Colaco et al.  54 ) to severe clinical conditions such as bacteremia (García et al.  75 ; Kato et al.  107 ) and multiple organ failure, which may result in death (Colaco et al.  54 ). Some strains also produce potent toxins, including emetic toxins (Stenfors Arnesen et al.  219 ; Kalbhenn et al.  104 ; Huang et al.  94 ). Conversely, several  Bacillus  species form beneficial relationships, acting as probiotics with therapeutic potential in the treatment of various diseases (Lahiri et al.  121 ; Dang et al.  55 ). Particularly notable are those that live as endophytes within plant tissues, establishing close associations with their host plants, and garnering interest for applications in agriculture (Marchut-Mikołajczyk et al.  144 ; Zou et al.  267 ), biotechnology, and biomedicine (Cardoso et al.  42 ; Mahgoub et al.  141 ).

Endophytic  Bacillus  species are members of the genus  Bacillus  that colonize the internal tissues of plants during at least part of their life cycle, typically without inducing disease, and interact closely with their hosts and surrounding microbial communities. These bacteria may establish intimate, transient, or stable associations with their host plants, and the outcomes of these interactions vary across an ecological spectrum (Anand et al.  10 ). These relationships can be mutualistic (Aydi-Ben-Abdallah et al.  18 ; Lastochkina et al.  124 ; Adeleke et al.  3 ; Peng et al.  179 ), but may also become conditionally pathogenic depending on genetic factors of both the bacterium and the plant, as well as environmental conditions.  Bacillus  spp. endophytes can provide several benefits to their hosts, including enhanced tolerance to abiotic stresses such as water deficit (El-Megeed et al.  67 ) and salinity (Bharti et al.  32 ), protection against phytopathogens (Shahzad et al.  206 ; Aydi-Ben-Abdallah et al.  18 ), and improved plant growth (Marchut-Mikołajczyk et al.  144 ; Zou et al.  267 ; Bharti et al.  32 ). These effects are mediated by the production of siderophores and lytic enzymes, in addition to the ability to solubilize essential nutrients, all of which contribute directly to plant health and performance. Owing to this multifunctional profile, endophytic Bacillus strains are increasingly regarded as promising plant growth-promoting bacteria in agriculture, especially for sustainable farming approaches. Outside the agronomic context, their biosynthetic potential, particularly in producing lytic enzymes and diverse bioactive metabolites, has also drawn considerable interest in biotechnology and biomedical research (Bodhankar et al.  37 ; Akter et al.  8 ; Abdel-Nasser et al.  1 ).

Given their broad ecological adaptability, functional diversity, and recurrent occurrence across multiple plant systems, endophytic species of the genus  Bacillus  represent a particularly informative model for investigating how generalist microorganisms establish functionally consistent associations with phylogenetically distant hosts. The objective of this review is to examine endophytic  Bacillus  not only as plant growth promoters, but also as active components of complex ecological systems whose performance emerges from the integration of functional genomics, metabolic plasticity, and environmental context. We first discuss classical and emerging mechanisms associated with plant growth promotion and interactions with cultivated plants, placing them within an ecological framework. Next, we examine the biosynthetic capacity of this bacterial genus and discuss the evolutionary implications of putative functional redundancy. We then address genomic and phenotypic plasticity, highlighting how environmental signals shape functional responses and ecological performance. From this perspective, we extend the discussion beyond conventional agricultural systems by exploring the role of endophytic  Bacillus  in native plant communities and ecological restoration. Finally, we integrate recent advances in comparative genomics and pangenomics to examine the evolutionary basis of the endophytic lifestyle and the functional diversity observed across  Bacillus  strains. These topics provide a conceptual framework linking genomic diversity, metabolic versatility, ecological interactions, and biotechnological applications of endophytic  Bacillus  spp.

sections.heading: Host specificity, functional plasticity, and molecular mechanisms in endophytic interactions between Bacillus spp. and plants
paragraphs: Bacillus  species with an endophytic lifestyle have been isolated from a wide variety of host plants, including cultivated, medicinal, and agricultural species from diverse ecosystems (Table  1 ). In addition to host diversity, these endophytic bacteria demonstrate the ability to colonize multiple plant organs and tissues, such as roots (Adeleke et al.  3 ), stems, leaves (Paz et al.  176 ), and seeds (Gond et al.  79 ). This broad ecological distribution highlights not only their remarkable functional adaptability but also their capacity to associate with phylogenetically distant plant groups. Such a pattern suggests the presence of conserved or convergent mechanisms among different  Bacillus  species and strains, potentially leading to functional redundancy in their symbiotic capabilities. However, despite being frequently regarded as generalist endophytes, successful colonization by  Bacillus  spp. is not entirely random. Host specificity is likely shaped by a combination of plant-derived chemical signals, tissue-specific environmental filters, microbial chemotaxis, adhesion mechanisms, and the ability of individual strains to perceive and respond to host metabolic cues (Mengistu  150 ). These factors influence whether a given strain can establish, persist, and express beneficial traits within a particular plant host. Despite their ecological relevance, the mechanisms that govern plant–endophyte interactions remain poorly understood. This is particularly true from evolutionary, genetic, and ecological perspectives. This knowledge gap becomes even more evident in the case of microorganisms considered generalists, such as  Bacillus  spp., which can be isolated from a wide variety of host plants and tissues, as shown in Table  1 . In general, it is understood that symbiosis between plants and microorganisms depends on specific recognition and interaction mechanisms (Bellés-Sancho et al.  28 ; Zadegan et al.  257 ), as if a given microorganism were evolutionarily associated with a particular plant species or with phylogenetically related species. This is typically observed in well-characterized cases, such as rhizobacteria in legumes (Wang et al.  236 ; Soyano et al.  215 ; Yang et al.  249 ) and mycorrhizal fungi (Tsiknia et al.  229 ). Furthermore, several studies indicate that plant tissues represent highly selective niches, where physicochemical barriers, the plant's developmental stage, and its defense system act as environmental filters shaping the composition of resident microbial communities (Dastogeer et al.  57 ; Lan et al.  122 ; Chen et al.  48 ). Within this context, an intriguing paradox emerges. If symbiotic mechanisms are indeed specific, how can we explain that a  Bacillus  species or strain isolated from the leaves of a plant belonging to family X is capable, when inoculated into the roots of a phylogenetically unrelated plant from family Y, of promoting root development and increasing aboveground biomass? Are we dealing with "promiscuous" endophytes that do not depend on a particular host species, but rather take advantage of the opportunity for association itself? Or do different species of  Bacillus  activate distinct molecular mechanisms, leading to functionally similar symbiotic outcomes in plants despite divergent regulatory pathways (Long et al.  138 )?. These questions remain largely open and highlight the need for comparative studies that seek to understand the patterns of symbiotic associations in  Bacillus . This topic has yet to be addressed in an integrated manner, considering not only a limited temporal or functional framework, but also exploring the genetic, molecular, and ecological landscape of these interactions.

With the advancement of sequencing technologies, recent genomic studies have aimed to identify candidate genes involved in the symbiosis between microorganisms and plants or plant growth-promoting genes (Wang et al.  236 ; Riesco et al.  192 ; Obeng et al.  165 ). Some authors suggest that the endophytic lifestyle may be linked to the number and diversity of biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs), as well as the presence of specific metabolic pathways that facilitate colonization, persistence within plant tissues, and/or induce plant growth promotion (Wang et al.  236 ; Adeleke et al.  3 ; Zeng et al.  259 ; Semenza et al., 2022). Additionally, several tools have been developed to associate genomic data with bacterial lifestyles and functionally relevant traits involved in plant interactions. Examples include bacLIFE (Guerrero-Egido et al.  84 ), PGPg_finder (Pellegrinetti et al.  178 ), and PLaBAse (Patz et al.  175 ), which classify genes based on functions directly or indirectly related to plant growth promotion (Fig.  1 ). These tools bridge genomic data with functional hypotheses, although experimental validation remains essential to confirm the ecological relevance of predicted traits. However, it is important to note that not all plant growth-promoting bacteria are endophytic, and not all endophytes promote plant growth. Although these in silico inferences and functional annotations derived from genomic analyses represent important progress, there is still a lack of experimental validation to determine whether these genes are truly responsible for an endophytic lifestyle. The presence of a gene in the genome does not ensure its expression or functional role under conditions required for symbiosis establishment. Fig. 1 Direct and indirect mechanisms of plant growth promotion mediated by endophytes of the genus  Bacillus . The figure illustrates the main direct (orange sector) and indirect (blue sector) effects attributed to  Bacillus  spp. endophytes in promoting plant growth. Image created using Canva.com Pro

Few experimental studies have explored the molecular mechanisms underlying interactions between endophytic  Bacillus  spp. and their host plants. Recent evidence indicates that both plant- and microbe-derived metabolites play pivotal roles in these interactions by functioning as chemical mediators (Kiddee et al.  112 ; Wang And Zhu  234 ; Ahmed et al.  5 ). For instance, in a model involving the citrus pathosystem and the pathogen  Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus  (CLas), the causative agent of Huanglongbing (HLB), surfactin produced by the endophyte  B. subtilis  L1–21 was shown to be essential for effective host colonization, activation of plant defense pathways, and modulation of the associated microbiome (Ahmed et al.  5 ). Surfactin-deficient mutants exhibited markedly reduced colonization efficiency and pathogen suppression, and failed to trigger key metabolic pathways associated with flavonoids, lignans, and volatile compounds. These findings highlight surfactin as a signaling molecule in this interaction. In addition to the role of surfactin, recent studies have expanded our understanding of the ecological and molecular dynamics between endophytic  Bacillus  and their host plants. For example, the strain  B. velezensis  S141 was found to enhance symbiosis between  Lotus japonicus  and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi ( Rhizophagus irregularis ), promoting fungal colonization, spore production, and improved uptake of nitrogen and phosphorus, even without relying on indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) as the primary signaling molecule (Kiddee et al.  112 ). This suggests that additional bacterial metabolites or signaling pathways are involved in modulating this tripartite interaction. Similarly,  B. velezensis  has been reported to induce systemic resistance in walnut ( Juglans  spp.) against  Colletotrichum gloeosporioides , by regulating hormone-mediated defense pathways involving salicylic, jasmonic, and abscisic acids, along with genes related to photosynthesis, phenylpropanoid metabolism, and antioxidant activity (Wang And Zhu  234 ).

These observations support the hypothesis that  Bacillus  spp. may utilize multiple, parallel molecular pathways to establish symbiotic relationships with diverse host plants. Despite differences in host identity, environmental conditions, and microbial genotype, these distinct mechanisms can converge on similar phenotypic outcomes, such as growth promotion, stress tolerance, or modulation of plant metabolism (Fig.  2 ). This functional convergence suggests a level of mechanistic plasticity that enables  Bacillus  spp. to act as generalists, while still responding in a context-dependent manner to specific plant partners. Understanding these convergent pathways is essential for elucidating the rules that govern microbe–plant compatibility and for the rational design of microbial inoculants tailored to diverse agricultural systems. Fig. 2 Schematic model representing the interaction between  Bacillus  and different plant hosts under distinct ecological contexts over time. In this example, a  Bacillus  species recognizes rhizosphere metabolites, performs chemotaxis, penetrates plant tissues by secreting enzymes, and colonizes the plant interior. Different host species (Fabaceae and Poaceae) are exposed to biotic stresses (fungi and bacteria) and abiotic stresses (drought and low nutrient availability).  Bacillus  colonization promotes plant growth through multiple direct and indirect mechanisms, including the production of antibiotics, hydrolytic enzymes, phytohormones, siderophores, and other bioactive metabolites, together with the modulation of plant metabolism and the induction of defense responses. Despite contextual differences, phenotypic outcomes converge toward enhanced vegetative development and biomass accumulation, highlighting the functional plasticity of the symbiosis and its relevance for plant growth promotion under diverse environmental conditions. sections.heading: Plant growth promotion by endophytic Bacillus spp.: mechanisms, methodological limitations, and agronomic relevance
paragraphs: Although the molecular, genetic, and ecological mechanisms regulating the interaction between  Bacillus  and its host plant remain poorly understood, the processes responsible for plant growth promotion resulting from this interaction have been more extensively studied and documented (Leite et al.  126 ; Falcão et al.  69 ; Chen et al.  47 ). Several literature reviews have addressed the role of endophytic bacteria in plant growth promotion from multiple perspectives, including physiological, genetic, ecological, and applied aspects, and across diverse environmental scenarios, such as abiotic stress, degraded soils, and intensive agricultural systems (Rana et al., 2020; Ali et al., 2024; Singh et al.  210 ). In this context, phenotypic screening of growth-promoting mechanisms has become a key step in the selection of strains with biotechnological potential for agricultural applications (Ji et al.  97 ; Li et al.  128 ; Chen et al.  47 ; Zou et al.  267 ). This screening includes, for example, the in vitro evaluation of phytohormone production, nutrient solubilization, siderophore synthesis, and antimicrobial activity, among other traits widely documented in the literature (Murugappan et al.  157 ; Khan et al.  109 ; Zou et al.  267 ). These mechanisms, classified as direct and indirect, as illustrated in Fig.  1 , are discussed below to provide an integrated understanding of the processes involved in plant growth promotion by endophytic  Bacillus  spp.

Among the direct mechanisms, the production of phytohormones such as indole-3-acetic acid (Khianngam et al.  110 ; Chebotar et al.  46 ), cytokinins (Lastochkina et al.  125 ), and gibberellins (Baliyan et al.  25 ) stands out, as these compounds modulate cell division, root elongation, and the development of the plant aerial system (Orozco-Mosqueda et al.  168 ). In parallel, the production of enzymes such as phosphatases, together with siderophores and nutrient-solubilizing compounds, increases the bioavailability of phosphorus, iron, and other essential minerals (Paz et al.  176 ; Chen et al.  47 ; Kushwaha et al.  119 ; Khan et al.,  108 a-b; Zou et al.  267 ). This biosynthetic capacity, observed in numerous endophytic  Bacillus  strains, directly contributes to increased plant biomass and improved physiological performance, both under optimal conditions and under stress (Paz et al.  176 ; Chen et al.  47 ; Kushwaha et al.  119 ; Khan et al.,  109 a-b; Zou et al.  267 ; Lastochkina et al.  125 ). In addition to these direct effects, endophytic  Bacillus  species can also promote plant growth through indirect mechanisms, mainly involving the suppression of phytopathogens and the modulation of the host plant’s defense responses. Antagonism toward phytopathogens by endophytic  Bacillus  spp. involves both chemical and enzymatic mechanisms. These include the production of antimicrobial lipopeptides and volatile organic compounds that restrict pathogen growth (Velho et al.  231 ; Asari et al.  16 ; Zhang et al.  262 ), as well as siderophore-mediated iron competition (Kim et al.  113 ). Additionally, the secretion of hydrolytic enzymes contributes to the breakdown of phytopathogen cell structures, impairing their colonization capacity (Li et al.  129 ). Furthermore, some  Bacillus  strains can induce systemic resistance in plants, promoting a “pre-activation” state of the plant defense system that results in greater tolerance to stress (Samaniego-Gámez et al.  200 ). These indirect effects not only reduce pathogen pressure in the rhizosphere and internal plant tissues, but also contribute to a more efficient allocation of plant resources, ultimately leading to increased growth and productivity.

However, the assays commonly used to evaluate direct and indirect growth-promoting mechanisms by endophytic  Bacillus  spp. are predominantly based on in vitro screenings, which often fail to capture the complexity and variability of natural or agricultural environments (Fig.  3 ). For example, although bacterial strains exhibiting direct/indirect plant growth-promoting mechanisms under controlled conditions often show consistent responses in laboratory assays, these phenotypes may fail to manifest, or may be expressed only to a limited extent, in greenhouse experiments or under field conditions, where environmental variability is substantially greater (Bacilio et al.  23 ; Hashmi et al.  89 ; Bizjak-Johansson et al.  35 ). This discrepancy arises because traditional screening methods do not adequately reproduce key factors such as microbial competition, actual resource availability, environmental fluctuations, and host plant responses (Hashmi et al.  89 ; Bizjak-Johansson et al.  35 ). Conceptual models based on increasing gradients of environmental complexity further suggest that, while systems analogous to in vitro assays exhibit low variance and high phenotypic reproducibility, higher complexity leads to increased variability and context-dependent expression, even when average effects remain relatively stable (Bacilio et al.  23 ; Westneat et al.  241 ; Spratt And Lane,  216 ; Leung et al.  127 ; Walter et al.  233 ). These patterns demonstrate the methodological limitations of directly extrapolating phenotypes observed in the laboratory, indicating that in vitro screenings primarily reflect the functional potential of  Bacillus  species, rather than their ecological stability or agronomic robustness under environmentally realistic conditions. Fig. 3 Conceptual model contrasting simplified in vitro screening assays for plant growth promotion by endophytic  Bacillus  spp. with the ecological complexity of natural and agricultural environments. Image created using Canva.com Pro

More recently, genomic approaches and other omics-based tools have been increasingly used to investigate the relationship between genotype and phenotype, including traits associated with plant growth promotion. Although still underexplored in studies focusing on endophytic  Bacillus  spp., these approaches hold considerable potential for future research. In general, they aim to associate genes, gene sets, and metabolic pathways with functional characteristics linked to bacterial lifestyle, such as the capacity to establish mutualistic interactions and promote plant growth. In this context, several computational platforms and analytical workflows have been developed to systematically explore large-scale genomic and metagenomic datasets. Notable examples include bacLIFE (Guerrero-Egido et al.  84 ), PGPg_finder (Pellegrinetti et al.  178 ), and PLaBAse (Patz et al.,  175 ).

These tools typically integrate steps such as genome dereplication, functional annotation, comparative genomics, and statistical or machine learning-based analyses to identify genes and gene clusters associated with specific lifestyles or plant growth-promoting traits. The bacLIFE framework, for instance, combines large-scale comparative genomics with predictive modeling to identify Lifestyle-Associated Genes (LAGs), taking into account both individual genes and biosynthetic gene clusters (Guerrero-Egido et al.  84 ). PGPg_finder was developed with a more targeted focus on identifying genetic determinants associated with plant growth promotion, allowing comparisons of gene and pathway distributions across bacterial genomes and metagenomic datasets (Pellegrinetti et al.  178 ). PLaBAse, in contrast, provides a centralized resource that integrates genomic information from plant-associated bacteria with predictive tools aimed at inferring growth-promoting traits and patterns of plant–bacterium association (Patz et al.,  175 ). It should be noted that, to date, the manuscript for the PLaBAse database and web tool is in preprint. In addition to these platforms, other workflows and resources aimed at predicting phenotypic traits from genomic data have also been proposed, including MicrobiotaProcess (Xu et al.  246 ,  247 ), the BactoTraits database (Cébron et al.  44 ), and machine learning-based models for phenotypic prediction based on genomic data (Koblitz et al.  116 ). The use of genome-based phenotypic prediction approaches can be combined with conventional screening methods, guiding the selection of targeted confirmatory assays for the presence of specific traits (Fig.  4 ). Fig. 4 Integrated in silico and in vitro screening framework for plant growth-promoting traits in endophytic  Bacillus  spp. The diagram shows how genome-based and phenotypic assays provide complementary information on growth-promoting mechanisms, supporting line selection and functional validation at increasing levels of biological complexity. Image created using Canva.com Pro

In general, and despite advances enabled by omics approaches, it is important to acknowledge that these tools, as well as in vitro phenotypic screenings, primarily describe the functional potential of microorganisms, rather than the consistent expression of these mechanisms in ecologically complex settings such as natural and agricultural systems. Although the integration of multiomics data improves the resolution of genotype–phenotype associations and provides valuable insights into metabolic and regulatory capacities, its predictive power remains constrained by environmental context, host specificity, and biotic interactions. Consequently, a robust understanding of plant growth promotion by endophytic  Bacillus  spp. depends on the combined use of molecular approaches to identify candidate mechanisms and their validation across multiple experimental scales.

sections.heading: A perspective on the genetic inventories provided by the pangenomics of Bacillus spp. and their functional outcomes
paragraphs: Genomic approaches can no longer be regarded as exceptional or outside routine practice, as they have become increasingly frequent and indispensable for the study of bacterial genomes (Land et al.  123 ; Loman and Pallen,  137 ; Eyre  68 ). In this context, pangenomics, understood as the integrated analysis of core and accessory genes within a species (Tettelin et al.  226 ), has also advanced substantially (Rouli et al.  194 ; Bach et al.  22 ; Zeng et al.  261 ), paralleling progress in studies of plant growth promoting bacteria (Saeed et al.  198 ; Aziz et al.  19 ; Ajdig et al.  7 ). Consequently, pangenomic analyses have become central to investigations of  Bacillus  diversity, largely driven by the rapid expansion of available genome sequences and by the broad ecological distribution of this genus (Chun et al.  53 ; Kadiri et al.  103 ; Bach et al.  22 ; Zeng et al.  261 ). While early studies primarily focused on classifying pangenomes as open or closed (Wang et al.  237 ,  237 ; Chun et al.  53 ), more recent work has emphasized that the main value of pangenomics lies not in gene counts, but in understanding how genetic variability translates into functional potential across distinct ecological contexts (Hyun et al.  95 ; Shoer et al.  209 ). From this perspective, pangenomics can be used to contextualize genetic diversity across multiple scales, linking different pangenomes to gene function across multiple species and levels of resolution, including pangenome structure, individual genes, sequence variants, and specific positions within those variants (Jonkheer et al.  101 ; Hyun et al.  95 ). For endophytic  Bacillus,  this approach is particularly relevant, as strains belonging to the same species and isolated from phylogenetically distant hosts often display similar plant growth promoting traits, despite exhibiting some genomic differences (Thanh Tam et al.  227 ). This functional convergence may indicate that distinct genetic routes can lead to comparable ecological outcomes, supported by different subsets of the pangenome that are selectively expressed in response to environmental conditions or host associated contexts.

Comparative genomic studies involving hundreds or thousands of  Bacillus  genomes consistently show that core genes are predominantly associated with essential cellular functions and central metabolism, whereas accessory genes are enriched in traits related to environmental sensing, secondary metabolism, and stress tolerance (Wu et al.  242 ; Wang et al.  239 ; Neal et al.  159 ; Acho-Vasquez et al.,  2 ). The distribution of many accessory genes varies among strains and lineages, often reflecting ecological specialization rather than phylogenetic relatedness (Wu et al.  242 ; Bach et al.  21 ,  21 ; Wang et al.  239 ; Acho-Vasquez et al.,  2 ; Patil et al.  174 ; Dushku et al.  66 ). This variability contributes to the remarkable genomic plasticity observed across  Bacillus  species. For example, pangenomic analyses of the  B. subtilis  species complex revealed that while core genes are largely associated with housekeeping functions, rare genes display lineage-specific functional profiles. In  B. subtilis , these genes are mainly related to DNA methylation and cellular regulation, whereas in  B. velezensis  they are enriched in biosynthetic pathways involved in lipopeptide production (Wang et al.  239 ).

Although pangenomic datasets have frequently been used to associate plant growth promotion or plant association with the presence or absence of specific genes and biosynthetic clusters (Zhou et al.  266 ; Ajdig et al.,  7 ; Gomes et al.  78 ), such interpretations should be approached cautiously. Gene detection alone does not guarantee expression or functionality under ecologically relevant conditions, and experimental validation remains essential to establish links between genomic variation and phenotypic traits. Furthermore, inaccurate strain identification and database deposition errors can artificially inflate estimates of pangenome diversity and distort interpretations of core and accessory genome composition (Wu et al.  242 ), Fig.  5 . Fig. 5 Conceptual overview linking endophytic  Bacillus  strains from the same species complex to pangenome structure and functional outcomes. Image created using Canva.com Pro

Beyond protein-coding genes, pangenomic studies increasingly consider the contribution of regulatory elements, single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), genomic islands, phages, and plasmids to functional diversity (Zeng et al.  258 ; Galardini et al.  74 ; Hollensteiner et al.  90 ; Beard et al.  27 ; Rauniyar et al.  187 ; Shaw et al.  207 ; Harrison et al.  88 ; Karampatakis et al.  106 ) (Fig.  6 ). Variations in promoter regions, transcriptional regulators, and global regulatory networks can substantially modify gene expression without altering gene content (Sojka et al.  212 ; Phan et al.  181 ; Arrieta-Ortiz et al.,  15 ; Mwita et al.  158 ; Anderson et al.  11 ). Consequently, strains sharing similar sets of plant growth-promoting genes may display distinct phenotypes depending on the host plant or environmental conditions. This pattern was observed in comparative genomic analyses of  B. cereus , where conserved plant growth-promoting genes co-occurred with SNP variation potentially associated with phenotypic differences among strains (Zeng et al.  258 ). Although most mutations were synonymous, nonsynonymous substitutions may contribute to adaptive and phenotypic divergence. Fig. 6 A Metabolomic and molecular networking workflow to explore the biosynthetic potential of  Bacillus . Image created using Canva.com Pro

Plasmids can also be regarded as critical components of bacterial adaptive and interaction capacities, although they remain underexplored in the context of pangenomic and comparative genomic analyses. These extrachromosomal elements frequently harbor genes involved in antibiotic production, resistance, metal tolerance, stress responses, and niche adaptation, and can be rapidly gained or lost through horizontal gene transfer, as discussed in several recent studies (Billane et al.  34 ; Newbury et al.  161 ; Benz And Hall,  30 ; Kiattisewee  111 ). Research focused on plasmids is well established in the field of health sciences, given their central role in the dissemination of resistance mechanisms in hospital and healthcare-associated environments (Pitout and Chen,  184 ; Ajayi et al.  6 ; Domingues et al.  63 ). More recently, however, there has been growing effort to integrate plasmid research into other areas of bacteriology, including the development of dedicated assembly pipelines and curated databases to support plasmid detection and analysis (Schmartz et al.  202 ; Bouras et al.  39 ). In plant-associated environments, plasmids have traditionally been studied mainly from pathogenic or transformation-related perspectives, such as those involving Agrobacterium plasmids (Hooykaas  91 ; Azizi-Dargahlou et al.,  20 ; Szarzanowicz et al.  223 ). Nevertheless, plasmids may also carry genetic information that facilitates the dissemination of traits enhancing colonization efficiency, competitiveness, or persistence within host tissues (Roy et al.  195 ; Deng et al.  61 ). Because plasmids are mobile genetic elements, their potential use to enhance plant growth promoting traits also represents a promising avenue for future applications (Phillips et al.  182 ; Li et al.,  133 a). In this sense, plasmids should be considered integral components of pangenomic and comparative genomic analyses, deserving greater attention in studies aimed at understanding the functional versatility and adaptive potential of bacterial populations (Peñil-Celis et al.  180 ; Sgro et al.,  203 ).

sections.heading: From biosynthetic potential to bioactive metabolites in Bacillus
paragraphs: The genus  Bacillus  is widely recognized for its high biosynthetic capacity, particularly for the production of secondary metabolites with antifungal and antibacterial activity (Kim et al.  114 ; Su et al.  220 ; Barale et al.  26 ; Sam-On et al.  201 ; Li et al.,  133 b; Qin et al.  185 ; Mahmud et al.,  143 ; Sousa et al.  214 ). Studies investigating the biosynthetic potential of  Bacillus  species based on genomic data, often using prediction tools such as antiSMASH (Medema et al.  147 ; Blin et al.  36 ), commonly focus on the analysis of BGCs from one or a limited number of strains (Barale et al.  26 ; Sam-On et al.  201 ; Li et al.,  133 b; Qin et al.  185 ). As a result, the understanding of presence–absence patterns and the evolutionary dynamics of these gene clusters remains limited. In contrast, large-scale genome mining studies indicate that a substantial fraction of the chemical repertoire of  Bacillus  spp. is composed of recurrent BGCs that are widely shared among phylogenetically related species (Steinke et al.  218 ; Song et al.  213 ; Stannius et al.  217 ). At the same time, the occurrence of clusters restricted to particular species or lineages points to a dynamic balance between evolutionary conservation and functional specialization (Zhao And Kuipers,  264 ; Grubbs et al.  81 ; Mullins et al.  155 ; Xia et al.  243 ; Yin et al.  251 ). This variability in biosynthetic repertoires likely contributes to the functional plasticity of endophytic  Bacillus  spp., enabling different strains to occupy distinct ecological niches, adapt to diverse plant-associated environments, and establish associations with a wide range of host plants. For instance, this relationship between phylogeny and biosynthetic repertoire was examined by Xia et al. ( 243 ) using comparative genomic analyses combined with experimental antagonism assays. The authors showed that phylogenetically close species tend to share similar sets of BGCs and, consequently, display lower levels of mutual antagonism.

In parallel, complementary evidence for this organization derived from the analysis of 1,500  Bacillus  genomes suggests that most identified BGCs are associated with a relatively small set of highly conserved metabolites, many of which are likely linked to central aspects of bacterial physiology, including the regulation of biofilm formation, cellular differentiation, and sporulation (Grubbs et al.  81 ). Experimental validation of the role of alkylpyrones in modulating sporulation in  B. subtilis  supports the idea that conserved BGCs tend to encode fundamental regulatory functions (Grubbs et al.  81 ). A more recent study based on the analysis of over 6,000 genomes from 66  Bacillus  species indicates that, although classes such as NRPS and RiPPs are broadly distributed across the genus, most BGC families and predicted metabolic scaffolds are species-specific (Yin et al.  251 ). Other genomic analyses of the biosynthetic capacity of  Bacillus  have examined the role of cytochrome P450 enzymes in shaping secondary metabolite structures and contributing to the chemical diversity observed within this bacterial group (Mthethwa et al.  153 ). In addition, recent evidence showing the ability of  Bacillus  strains to produce a melanin-like pigment suggests that even widely conserved BGCs may have originated through duplication and neofunctionalization of primary metabolism genes, with expression dependent on environmental context (Stannius et al.  217 ).

From the perspective of advancing our understanding of biosynthetic capacity, genome mining analyses encompassing hundreds or thousands of genomes have provided consistent evidence of the extensive biosynthetic potential of  Bacillus  (Grubbs et al.  81 ; Xia et al.  243 ; Yin et al.  251 ; Song et al.  213 ; Stannius et al.  217 ). From a more applied standpoint, however, several studies have focused on the metabolites that are effectively produced, aiming to characterize their chemical nature and biological activities. These investigations often begin with the detection of bioactive effects in in vitro assays and subsequently integrate different omics approaches, such as metabolomics and transcriptomics, to explore the chemical diversity associated with this bacterial genus (Cao et al.  41 ; Jayakumar et al.  96 ; Tsalgatidou et al.  228 ; Arriel-Elias et al.  14 ; Lagzian et al.  120 ; Singh et al.  210 ; Ahmed et al.  5 ; Chen et al.  49 ). Although frequently limited to single strains or a small number of isolates, these studies have made a substantial contribution to the functional understanding of the biosynthetic potential of  Bacillus . In this context, several metabolites have already been identified, and their biological activities have been experimentally validated. For instance, the lipopeptides fengycin and surfactin exhibit antifungal activity against organisms from distinct taxonomic groups (Jin et al.  100 ; Yousfi et al.  253 ; Wang et al.  240 ), including species of  Monilinia  and  Aspergillus  (Caretta et al.  43 ). Similarly, difficidin and bacillaene have been shown to inhibit the growth of  Fusarium graminearum  (Sun et al.,  222 ). Macrolactins, in turn, have been associated with reduced growth of  Botrytis cinerea  (Ni et al.  163 ),  F. oxysporum , and  Rhizoctonia solani  (Pandey et al.  171 ). In addition, bacillibactin has been primarily linked to antibacterial activity, consistent with its role in iron acquisition and competitive interactions within microbial communities (Chakraborty et al.  45 ; Pedroza-Padilla et al.  177 ). These findings reinforce the potential of the genus  Bacillus  as a source of bioactive molecules, with direct implications for industrial, pharmaceutical, and agricultural applications. Moreover, the diversity of bioactive compounds produced by endophytic  Bacillus  spp. reflects how genomic variation can translate into distinct ecological functions, helping explain the remarkable adaptability, host-associated interactions, and functional versatility observed among endophytic strains.

Metabolomics approaches allow a comprehensive view of the different types of metabolites produced, especially when integrated into hyphenated workflows that combine chromatographic methods with mass spectrometry and are coupled to molecular networking tools such as GNPS ( https://gnps.ucsd.edu/ProteoSAFe/ ) (Wang et al.  235 ; Aron et al.  13 ) and, more recently, GNPS2 ( https://gnps2.org/homepage ) (Yu et al.  255 ) (Fig.  5 ). This set of approaches enables a broader and more detailed characterization of the produced metabolome (Wang et al.  238 ; Xia et al.  244 ; Chen et al.  49 ). For example, analyses based on mass spectrometry and molecular networking enabled the characterization of the metabolome of four plant growth–promoting  Bacillus  strains, both individually and under co-culture conditions, revealing 11 differential molecular families composed of lipids and lipid-like molecules, benzenoids, nucleotide-related compounds, and organic acids and their derivatives (Nephali et al.  160 ). In this study, the metabolic profiles of the consortium and  B. amyloliquefaciens  were characterized by a high abundance of surfactins, whereas  B. licheniformis  strains showed the exclusive presence of lichenisins. Metabolomics-based approaches are therefore particularly promising for understanding the biosynthetic capacity of  Bacillus  and, although still underexplored, for evaluating the metabolic changes that plant growth–promoting strains can induce in the host plant (Vinci et al.  232 ; Liu et al.  136 ; Singh et al.  211 ).

sections.heading: Ecological consequences of Bacillus inoculation on plant-associated microbial communities
paragraphs: When we refer to plant growth–promoting bacteria, this concept is usually linked to their ability to establish ecological relationships with the host plant. This perspective is essential, as plants are no longer viewed as isolated organisms but rather as complex systems capable of hosting numerous other organisms in endophytic and or epiphytic associations, including fungi and bacteria (Choi et al.  51 ; Panebianco et al.  172 ; Ghazi-Yaker et al.  77 ; Mukhebi et al.  154 ; dos Reis et al.  64 ). From this standpoint, plants can be understood as plant holobionts that continuously evolve together with their microbiome (Mesny et al.  151 ; Berg et al.  31 ; Adomako et al.  4 ). Species of  Bacillus  have frequently been isolated as components of these resident microbial communities across different plant species and tissues (Table  1 ), indicating that this group of microorganisms is widely distributed and recurrent. However, from a practical perspective and under natural conditions, the abundance of these microorganisms is regulated by a dynamic balance shaped by environmental, genetic, and evolutionary factors, in addition to interactions and competition for resources and niche space (See the review by Pierce and Dutton, [ 183 ]), where some of these aspects are discussed.). In contrast, discussions on plant growth–promoting bacteria often assume the inoculation of very large numbers of bacterial cells, a practice that may disrupt the architecture of pre-established microbial communities in plant tissues or in the rhizosphere, with potential consequences for plant health (Kong and Liu,  117 ; Shi et al.  208 ).

When an endophytic or rhizospheric  Bacillus  strain is inoculated and successfully establishes within the target organ or tissue, this microorganism begins to interact with native microbial communities that were previously structured in that environment (García-Giraldo et al.  76 ; Liang et al.  134 ). The strength and nature of these interactions depend on multiple factors, including strain identity, the underlying interaction mechanisms, which may be direct or mediated by environmental modifications, and the cell density achieved after establishment. Together, these factors can influence the organization of resident communities, leading to changes in species richness and in the taxonomic and functional diversity observed prior to inoculation (Fig.  7 ; Table  2 ). Fig. 7 Conceptual structural model illustrating the ecological consequences of  Bacillus  inoculation on plant-associated microbial communities. The model highlights how  Bacillus  inoculation interacts with ecological context, including soil properties, resident microbiome composition, strain identity, and inoculum density, shaping community-level responses. These responses may involve changes in taxonomic structure, expressed through alpha and beta diversity patterns, and functional responses, including metabolic activity, gene expression, and enzyme activity. Such processes influence microbial interaction networks, which may be strengthened, weakened, or reorganized. Experimental studies have shown that  Bacillus  spp. inoculation can induce detectable shifts in microbial community structure, although such effects are not always consistently captured across different diversity metrics. The inoculation of  B. subtilis  in cotton, for instance, promoted yield increases and induced changes in bacterial and fungal communities at the level of beta diversity, while no significant differences were detected in alpha diversity metrics (Ren et al.  191 ). These findings suggest that inoculation may reorganize community composition without necessarily affecting overall taxon richness or abundance distribution. In addition,  B. subtilis  has been shown to interact with soil physicochemical properties, enzymatic activity, and microbial interaction networks, indicating that its effects extend beyond host colonization. Similarly, the inoculation of a different  B. subtilis  strain in chrysanthemum enhanced ecological interactions between bacteria and fungi, an effect attributed to positive impacts on host plant development (Tao et al.  225 ). In contrast, the co-inoculation of  Bradyrhizobium japonicum  and  B. aryabhattai  caused pronounced shifts in the taxonomic composition of soil microbial communities, with patterns varying according to soil type (Zhao et al.  265 ). These results highlight the role of edaphic context in shaping both the establishment success and ecological impact of inoculated microorganisms. Nevertheless, the absence of detectable changes in community structure has also been reported. The inoculation of  B. velezensis  in sugarcane, for example, did not result in significant differences in the richness or abundance of bacterial taxa in the rhizosphere (de Alcântara Neto et al.  58 ). It is important to note, however, that this study did not assess treatment effects using beta diversity metrics based on Bray–Curtis or Jaccard distances, nor did it apply permutational approaches to test for community-level differences. This methodological limitation precludes a more robust evaluation of potential compositional shifts and constrains direct comparisons with other studies.

The potential impacts of microbial inoculants on native or pre established microbial communities have been widely discussed (see Li et al.  131 ). However, it is important to emphasize that there is no universal response pattern, since this biological system is inherently complex and context dependent (Mawarda et a.,  146 ; Han et al.  86 ). This context dependence is consistently supported by studies evaluating the inoculation of different  Bacillus  strains under distinct environmental and edaphic conditions (Zhao et al.  265 ; de Alcântara Neto et al.  58 ; Tao et al.  225 ). For instance, increases in species richness may occur following inoculation, but higher richness does not necessarily imply a greater proportion of beneficial microorganisms and may also involve the proliferation of potentially pathogenic taxa. Conversely, community simplification, here defined as a reduction in species richness, may be advantageous under certain ecological contexts, while being detrimental under others. The opposite scenario is also possible, reinforcing that changes in richness alone are insufficient to infer ecological outcomes. In this context, interaction network analyses represent a valuable complementary approach, as they provide an in silico perspective on community organization, including interaction modules and potential correlations among microbial taxa (Reis et al.  188 ; Tao et al.  225 ). Similarly, beta diversity analyses are essential for evaluating community level responses to inoculation (Zhao et al.  265 ; Tao et al.  225 ). Although not always integrated, the combined use of presence absence based metrics, such as Jaccard, and abundance based metrics, such as Bray Curtis, allows the identification of whether observed differences are driven by taxon turnover or by shifts in relative abundance (Reis et al.  188 ).

Another key aspect that remains largely neglected in studies involving endophytic or rhizospheric  Bacillus  inoculants is the lack of functional interpretation. Microbial communities may show limited or no changes in taxonomic or phylogenetic composition while exhibiting substantial variation in functional profiles (Bennett et al.  29 ). Here, the opposite can also be observed (Zeng et al.  260 ). For example, analyses of fungal functional attributes have revealed functional redundancy along environmental gradients (Moreira et al.  152 ), a pattern that may also emerge in fungal communities following  Bacillus  inoculation. Alternatively, functional profiles may be reshaped without corresponding taxonomic shifts. Although fungal communities provide a clear illustration, similar patterns can be observed in bacterial communities (Yu And Whalen,  254 ). The inoculation of  B. thuringiensis , for instance, improved soybean development and increased soil functional diversity (Fonseca de Souza et al.  71 ). In this regard, transcriptomic and metabolomic approaches offer additional resolution by integrating information on gene expression patterns and metabolite production, thereby advancing the understanding of how inoculants modulate microbial functions at multiple biological levels (Nong et al.  164 ; Yuan et al.  256 ).

sections.heading: Endophytic Bacillus in non-agricultural systems: opportunities and ecological considerations
paragraphs: Historically, studies involving endophytic  Bacillus  spp. have been largely focused on agricultural crops of immediate economic interest, with an emphasis on growth promotion, yield enhancement, and the control of phytopathogens (Bai et al.  24 ; Huang et al.  92 ; Kang et al.  105 ; Mun et al.  156 ). Although this approach is highly relevant for agricultural systems, it has limited the understanding of the ecological role and broader potential of these microorganisms to highly managed environments, often simplified, such as monocultures, and subjected to strong anthropogenic pressures. In recent years, however, there has been a growing interest in exploring the potential of endophytic  Bacillus  in nonconventional contexts, including their association with native plant species from threatened biomes or with plant species at risk of extinction (Liu et al.  135 ; Oliveira et al.  166 ; Faria et al.  70 ), and in their application in ecological restoration projects in ecosystems exposed to different forms of stress resulting from land use and land use change (De-Bashan et al.  60 ; Rong et al.  193 ; Huang et al.,  93 a).

The use of the endophytic strain  B. thuringiensis  in combination with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi significantly increased the biomass of  Lavandula dentata  and mitigated the effects of water stress (Armada et al.  12 ). These findings highlight the potential of this microbial association as a strategy for restoring vegetation cover in arid and degraded soils. Another example highlighting the ecological relevance of endophytic  Bacillus  strains is the application of  B. amyloliquefaciens  CSUFTCSP75 in the recovery of forest soils impacted by pest infestations (Yang et al.  250 ). The introduction of this bacterium into degraded soils resulted in greater nutrient availability, particularly of phosphorus and potassium, while also stimulating microbial metabolic processes. Furthermore, treated soils retained a broader range of microbial functions, suggesting that this strain may contribute not only to nutrient cycling but also to the restoration of soil ecological processes and resilience (Yang et al.  250 ). Similarly,  Bacillus  strains have been employed in combination with other plant growth-promoting bacteria to enhance soil quality and facilitate vegetation establishment in forest reserves (Ramachandran & Radhapriya  186 ). Although positive effects on plant performance were reported, the authors did not indicate whether the bacterial strains were originally isolated as endophytes, despite being native to the restoration site. Nevertheless, this does not preclude the possibility that Bacillus strains establish endophytic associations after inoculation and subsequently contribute to plant growth promotion under degraded environmental conditions.

From the perspective of seedling production for ecological restoration, species of the genus  Bacillus  represent a promising tool for improving the establishment of native plants. Unlike agricultural crops, seeds of wild species are rarely subjected to treatment protocols to reduce pathogen loads and enhance germination (Owen And Powles,  169 ; Sabanci et al.  196 ; Goulart  80 ; Sagarika et al.  199 ). As a result, fungal contamination, low germination rates, and poor seedling establishment are common constraints in restoration programs (Martins et al.  145 ; Bruschet et al.  40 ; dos Santos et al.  65 ). Endophytic  Bacillus  spp. have been shown to enhance seed viability and germination (Lastochkina et al.  125 ; Tang et al.  224 ), suppress seed-borne pathogens (Kumar et al.  118 ; Newcombe et al.  162 ), and improve plant performance under biotic and abiotic stresses (Zhang et al.  263 ; Tu et al.  230 ; Mahmood et al.  142 ). For example, an endophytic strain of  B. subtilis  was shown to inhibit the growth of  Neodeightonia phoenicum  and  Penicillium purpurogenum , two fungal species associated with seed deterioration in  Butia purpurascens , a native plant species of the Brazilian Cerrado (Oliveira et al.  166 ). Therefore, integrating endophytic  Bacillus  into seedling production protocols may increase the success of restoration initiatives based on native plant species.

Although the application of  Bacillus  as an ecological restoration strategy appears promising, it raises questions that extend beyond plant growth promotion. Unlike agricultural systems, native ecosystems are characterized by high biological complexity, multispecies interactions, and a distinct evolutionary history linking plants and their associated microbial communities (Luo et al.  140 ; de Oliveira Silva et al.  59 ; Klein et al.  115 ). Within this context, the introduction of exogenous microorganisms prompts issues that remain insufficiently explored. How do these microorganisms affect the organization of soil biotic networks? In what ways might such interactions influence key ecosystem functions, including nutrient cycling and system stability? Can inoculation alter plant community composition, thereby affecting patterns of diversity, establishment, and species persistence? Moreover, could these changes propagate through trophic chains, generating indirect effects across multiple levels of the biota? Although many of these questions remain hypothetical, they underscore the importance of broader and more rigorous ecological assessments regarding the use of microbial inoculants in both natural environments.

sections.heading: Final considerations
paragraphs: This review examines the genus  Bacillus , particularly endophytic strains, as a system for investigating how metabolically versatile and genomically plastic bacteria establish functional, context-dependent associations with plants. Evidence from genomic, metabolomic, pangenomic, and ecological studies indicates that the performance of endophytic  Bacillus  is not explained by isolated traits or single mechanisms, but by interactions among genetic repertoires, regulatory processes, environmental conditions, and host-specific responses. In both agricultural and non-agricultural systems, these bacteria have been associated with plant growth promotion, increased stress tolerance, and shifts in plant-associated microbiomes. However, similar functional outcomes can arise from different genomic and metabolic configurations. Comparative and pangenomic analyses indicate that these phenotypes may be supported by distinct combinations of core and accessory genes, regulatory elements, mobile genetic elements, and biosynthetic gene clusters, supporting the view that plant growth promotion by  Bacillus  is conditional and context dependent.

A recurring issue discussed in this review is the limitation of in vitro screening approaches, which tend to reflect functional potential rather than ecological performance in complex environments. Although phenotypic assays and genome-based predictions remain useful for strain selection, their predictive value decreases when applied to systems shaped by biotic interactions, resource competition, and environmental heterogeneity. Addressing this limitation requires experimental validation across multiple biological scales, including greenhouse and field studies, combined with integrative omics approaches that capture functional activity rather than gene presence alone. From an ecological perspective, the intentional inoculation of  Bacillus  strains raises questions that extend beyond plant performance. Available evidence indicates that inoculation can modify resident microbial communities, alter interaction networks, and affect functional profiles, with outcomes that vary according to environmental context. These effects may be neutral, beneficial, or disruptive, particularly when inoculants are introduced at high densities into complex and evolutionarily structured microbiomes. For this reason, the ecological consequences of  Bacillus  inoculation should be considered explicitly in both agricultural and restoration contexts.

Finally, the application of  Bacillus -based strategies to non-agricultural systems, including ecological restoration and the propagation of native plant species, warrants careful evaluation. In such settings, endophytic  Bacillus  may influence seed germination, seedling establishment, and early plant performance under stress, but the introduction of exogenous microorganisms into native ecosystems requires evidence-based approaches that account for long-term ecological interactions and potential cascading effects.
